title: Building and Deploying
summary: Create a production build with ng build, configure environments, serve the browser folder from a static host or nginx with a fallback to index.html, run the SSR server, and automate it all in CI.
introduction: Development is done when the app runs on a URL other people can open. A production build turns your TypeScript into a handful of hashed files that any web server can serve, but single-page apps have one requirement that static hosts do not meet by default: every URL must fall back to index.html. This lesson builds the app, separates development and production settings, deploys to a static host and to nginx, runs the server-side rendered version, and sets up a workflow that tests and builds on every push.
learningObjectives: Produce and inspect a production build with ng build
Configure per-environment settings with file replacements
Deploy the browser output to a static host or nginx with an index.html fallback and run the SSR server

blocks.text: `ng build` uses the `production` configuration by default: it bundles with esbuild, minifies, removes unused code, inlines critical CSS and adds a content hash to every file name so browsers can cache them forever. The output goes to `dist/<project>/`.

blocks.text: The files you deploy are the ones inside `browser/`. `index.html` references the hashed files, so every release produces new names and old cached copies are never served by mistake. `ng build --configuration development` produces an unminified build with source maps for debugging a deployment problem.

blocks.title: Common mistake: deploying the wrong folder
blocks.text: Uploading `dist/my-app` instead of `dist/my-app/browser` puts `index.html` one level too deep: the site root shows a directory listing or a 404 while `/browser/` works. Point the host at the `browser` folder. With SSR enabled there is also a `server/` folder next to it, which static hosts must not serve.

API URLs and feature flags differ between your machine and production. The CLI handles this with **file replacements**: `ng generate environments` creates two files and tells `angular.json` to swap one for the other in development builds. Import from `environment.ts` everywhere; the build picks the right file.

blocks.text: Never put secrets in environment files: everything in the browser bundle is public. Secrets belong on the server; the browser only ever gets a session token.
Static hosting and the fallback rule

A client-rendered Angular app is just static files, so any static host works: Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Firebase Hosting, an S3 bucket, or your own nginx. All of them need one rule: a request for `/products/42` must return `index.html`, because the file `products/42` does not exist and the Angular router will read the URL once the app loads. Without that rule, reloading any page other than the home page gives a 404.

blocks.title: /etc/nginx/conf.d/my-app.conf
curl -I http://localhost/products/42
blocks.content:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Content-Type: text/html

blocks.text: `try_files` serves a real file when one exists (the hashed JavaScript and CSS) and `index.html` for everything else. The cache header is safe because the file names change whenever their content changes. Other hosts express the same rule in their own files:

rows: No rewrites available: build with `--base-href /repo-name/` and copy `index.html` to `404.html`

blocks.text: Files placed in the project's `public/` folder are copied to the build output unchanged, which is where `_redirects`, `robots.txt` and similar files live. When the app is served from a sub-path, `ng build --base-href /my-app/` sets the `<base href>` so that relative URLs and the router resolve correctly.

With `@angular/ssr` added, `ng build` also produces `dist/my-app/server/server.mjs`, a Node application that renders pages on request and serves the browser files. Run it on any host that supports Node.js: a container, a virtual machine or a platform such as Render, Railway or Fly.io. The fallback rule is handled by the server itself.

blocks.content: Node Express server listening on http://localhost:4000

blocks.text: Routes marked for prerendering in `app.routes.server.ts` are rendered to static HTML at build time, so a marketing page costs nothing per request while a personalised dashboard still renders on demand. A `Dockerfile` for the server needs only `node:24-alpine`, the `dist` folder and `CMD ["node", "dist/my-app/server/server.mjs"]`; the [Docker tutorial](/tutorials/docker) covers the details.

A workflow that installs dependencies, runs the tests and builds on every push catches broken builds before they reach a server. This [GitHub Actions](/tutorials/github-actions) workflow does exactly that; `ng test` and `ng build` exit with a non-zero code on failure, which marks the run as failed.

blocks.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml
blocks.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx ng test
      - run: npx ng build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: browser
          path: dist/my-app/browser

blocks.text: `npm ci` installs exactly the versions in `package-lock.json`, so the build on the server matches the one on your machine. The uploaded artifact is what a deploy step copies to the host; many hosts can also watch the repository and run the build themselves.

blocks.title: ng deploy
blocks.text: Hosting providers publish deploy builders: after `ng add @angular/fire` or `ng add angular-cli-ghpages`, a single `ng deploy` builds and uploads the app. They are convenient for personal projects; for team projects, keep the deployment in the CI workflow where everyone can see it.
